llm.summary: The skill implements a coherent local audit/snapshot/rollback system, but it requires broad access to files and commands, exposes a web UI with no documented authentication, and has some implementation issues that materially increase risk — review carefully before integrating it into OpenClaw or a production host.

dimensions.detail: The code and instructions match the stated purpose: auditing tool calls, creating git-based snapshots, a web dashboard, permission rules, and rollback. The requirement to hook into OpenClaw's execution path and provide a shell wrapper is expected for a system that claims to capture 'all operations'.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Runtime instructions and scripts ask you to (a) start a web server (server_v2.py) that serves dashboard and rollback actions, (b) integrate the auditor into OpenClaw's tool call flow (wrapping/replace tool execution), and (c) optionally add a shell alias to route commands through an audit wrapper. Those instructions allow the skill to see/record arbitrary command text, file contents (audited_read), and other sensitive data — and there is no documented authentication or remote-access restriction for the web UI. The audit wrapper also evals provided command strings (expected but risky).
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: This is an instruction-only skill with bundled scripts; there is no network-based installer, no downloaded third-party binary, and no package install specified. Risk from install mechanism is low, but the skill writes persistent artifacts to ~/.openclaw (database and git snapshots).
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill does not request environment credentials, which is consistent. However, to deliver its function it requires broad filesystem access (reading/writing many user and system paths, snapshots under ~/.openclaw/snapshots, and a local DB at ~/.openclaw/audit.db). That level of access is proportional for a system-level auditor but increases the risk surface (sensitive files may be captured and stored unencrypted).
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: The skill persistently stores audit data and snapshots in ~/.openclaw and runs a persistent web server allowing rollback actions. It does not set always:true, which is good, but the web UI and API endpoints are served locally without documented authentication or authorization. Persistent presence plus unauthenticated admin actions (restore/rollback) is a significant operational risk.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance: This skill largely does what it says (audit + snapshots + rollback) but it grants broad read/write access to your filesystem and stores potentially sensitive contents and snapshots locally. Before installing or integrating: 1) Review server_v2.py / server_simple.py for any network listeners and add authentication (HTTP auth or local-only socket) to the web UI — do not expose the dashboard to a network interface. 2) Treat the DB (~/.openclaw/audit.db) and snapshots (~/.openclaw/snapshots/) as sensitive: set strict permissions, consider encryption, and inspect what is logged (file contents may be stored). 3) Avoid enabling automatic integration into OpenClaw or shell aliasing in production until you audit the code; wrapping all tool calls gives the skill visibility into every operation and could leak secrets into logs. 4) Note implementation issues: audit_wrapper.sh's permission check prints a lowercase 'true' but compares to 'True' (likely causing unintended denials), and wrapper uses eval on user-supplied command strings (expected for a wrapper but dangerous if the wrapper itself is modified). 5) Run first in an isolated/test environment, review and harden permission rules, add authentication/authorization for the web UI, and ensure rollbacks are gated (confirm prompts, dry-run). If you don't have capacity to review the code yourself, treat this skill as high-risk and avoid integrating it into environments that hold secrets or critical systems.
